Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> National | Opinion Engineering Ghana’s automotive and transport transformation: From import dependence to industrial growth Source : Sadik Koli Abdul Rahim 23 October 2026 5:18pm Audio By Carbonatix
Ghana’s automotive and transport sectors hold enormous potential for industrialisation, job creation, investment and economic growth. Realising this potential requires a shift from dependence on imported vehicles and reactive transport management towards local engineering, evidence-based planning, manufacturing and effective regulation.
Ghana must move beyond vehicle assembly to vehicle design, component manufacturing, testing and production. We should connect universities, technical universities, Ghanaian engineers and local businesses with established international manufacturers to design and prototype vehicles suited to Ghanaian conditions—from affordable utility vehicles to agricultural and commercial transport. International partnerships should deliver manufacturing technology, quality assurance and skills transfer, while government incentives reward local content, employment and technology development. Successful products can serve Ghana and expand into African markets through the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).
Institutions such as the Ghana Automotive Development Centre must have the funding, skilled personnel and technical capacity to develop and implement internationally aligned policies. Applicable vehicle import and safety standards must be consistently enforced. Vehicles that fail the relevant requirements should be rejected or otherwise handled through lawful procedures. Consumer protection, roadworthiness and public safety must take priority.
Ghana needs stronger verification and traceability of spare parts, particularly safety-critical components such as brakes, steering and suspension. Dealers should be supported in building relationships with reputable OEMs and legitimate aftermarket suppliers. Using DVLA registration data alongside vehicle age, component compatibility, failure rates and market demand would help guide imports towards parts needed by the active vehicle fleet. This can reduce unsuitable stock, improve availability and protect consumers from counterfeit or defective components, while assessing used parts according to their actual condition and safety.
We cannot effectively manage congestion without understanding passenger movements. Ghana needs reliable data on travel origins and destinations, passenger numbers, vehicle occupancy, routes, traffic volumes and journey times across different days and hours. For example, analysing travel between Kasoa and central Accra could help determine the right public transport capacity, routes and service frequency. Traffic surveys, GPS fleet data and responsibly managed digital information can guide planning, while Ghanaian technology companies develop useful commuter applications. Engineering studies should inform dedicated bus lanes, improved interchanges, coordinated traffic signals and better pedestrian facilities—avoiding both inadequate services and unnecessary oversupply.
Ghana recorded 2,949 road deaths, 14,743 crashes and 16,714 injuries in 2025, with fatalities increasing by 18.2% compared with 2024. We need coordinated action through safer road and junction design, effective enforcement, vehicle inspections, preventive fleet maintenance, proper drainage, visible road markings, pedestrian protection and reliable emergency response.
High-risk locations must be identified and interventions prioritised using crash data and measurable safety benefits. While major infrastructure programmes such as the Big Push are important, urban roads, traffic management and integrated public transport must also receive sustained attention. Short-term local initiatives cannot replace long-term planning of Ghana’s road networks and mobility systems.
Ghana needs a coordinated national approach that brings together automotive manufacturing, engineering education, institutional reform, vehicle and spare-parts standards, transport data and safer infrastructure. These are connected challenges requiring practical, measurable solutions—not isolated interventions.
Our ambition must be greater than importing vehicles or easing traffic. It must be to build Ghanaian engineering capability, create local industrial value, reduce congestion, save lives, and establish Ghana as a competitive automotive and transport hub for Africa.
